ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows an operational amplifier circuit. The input terminal is on the left; the upper branch is connected through capacitor C to the inverting input terminal of the op-amp; the output terminal is fed back through resistor R to the same inverting input node. The lower branch is connected through capacitor C to the non-inverting input terminal, and this non-inverting input node is then connected to ground through resistor R, serving as the reference branch. The right-side output is labeled Vo, and the input phasor is labeled Vi with phase 0. Reasoning: Treat it as an ideal op-amp, and calculate according to the inverting structure. The impedance of the inverting input branch is the capacitor impedance Z_C = 1/(jωC), and the feedback impedance is Z_f = R. Therefore the voltage gain is Vo/Vi = -Z_f/Z_C = -R/(1/(jωC)) = -jωRC. Since ω, R, and C are all positive real numbers, the phase angle of -jωRC is -π/2. The input phase is 0 rad, so the output phase δ = -π/2 rad.

method.method_draft: Start by interpreting the diagram as a virtual-ground inverting differentiator: the non-inverting input fixes the reference, and the inverting node is held at the same potential. Write KCL at the inverting node in the time domain: the current through the input capacitor C must flow through the feedback resistor R, leading to v_o(t)=-RC dv_i(t)/dt. For an input phasor with phase 0, take v_i(t)=V_i cos(ωt). Then -RC dv_i/dt is proportional to sin(ωt), which equals cos(ωt-π/2). Thus the output lags the input by π/2, so δ=-π/2.
